after.en: Each pixel is worked out on its own, leaving the others alone. This is a per-pixel operation: it changes brightness, but never knows who its neighbours are.

t.en: On a film camera's negative, light and dark are reversed: the sky looks black and a white shirt looks dark. Printing reverses them again to bring the picture back to normal. Doctors reading X-rays also often switch between positive and negative.
In a digital image, inverting means replacing the number in every cell: 0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0, 0.3 becomes 0.7. The photo is still the same photo, just with light and dark swapped.

Why "1 minus the input"? Brightness always lies between 0 and 1. Multiply each cell by −1 alone and a dark 0.3 becomes −0.3 while a bright 0.9 becomes −0.9: light and dark are swapped, but every number has dropped below 0, darker than black. Add 1 to every cell and the whole picture is lifted back into 0 … 1: −0.3 + 1 = 0.7 and −0.9 + 1 = 0.1. So "multiply by −1, then add 1" is 1 − input: what was brighter is now darker.

The parts in this level are all simple: <part-ref to="part:const"></part-ref> always outputs the same number; <part-ref to="part:mul"></part-ref> and <part-ref to="part:add"></part-ref> multiply and add two things cell by cell. When a number meets a picture, the number applies to every cell.
Your task in this level: using only these multiplications and additions, make "1 minus the input".

caption.en: Set 1: a square and its negative

brief.en: Black becomes white, white becomes black: output = 1 − input.

hint.en: First multiply every number by −1, then add one number to all of them.
